title: Licensed alternatives: Expanded practice retains accountability
desc: Compares bounded nonlawyer routes that preserve competence assessment, client protection and escalation when authorized scope becomes insufficient.

kps.k: The cluster presents alternative routes into legal practice that retain licensing and accountability rather than remove regulation.
kps.d: The frameworks change different boundaries: Texas’s preliminarily approved rules authorize limited nonlawyer services for low-income clients; Oregon’s final rules approved on 7 November 2023 establish a supervised portfolio route to lawyer admission; Arizona’s R-20-0034 assigns licensing and disciplinary responsibilities for legal paraprofessionals and alternative business structures. These are distinct reforms to practice scope, admission assessment and provider governance—not interchangeable models or permissions for AI systems to practise law.

kps.k: Texas ties expanded nonlawyer practice to client eligibility, defined tasks and selective lawyer involvement.
kps.d: The preliminary framework limits clients to those at or below 200% of federal poverty guidelines and offers family, estate-planning and probate, and consumer-debt licenses rather than general licensure. Any subject license nevertheless permits independent representation in justice-court civil suits. Elsewhere, permissions narrow: independent divorce work excludes children and complex property issues, while specified uncontested protection and parent–child matters require supervision. Supervisors review documents before filing and remain available for questions but need not attend hearings. Immigration services remain prohibited. Providers therefore need intake and scope-screening processes, not merely a subject credential.

kps.k: Alternative entry routes retain competence assessment, but Texas and Oregon assess different forms of practice readiness.
kps.d: Texas accepts several education, credential and experience routes, then adds subject-specific qualifications, ethics testing, subject examinations subject to exemptions, and character-and-fitness review. Oregon requires 675 hours, at least eight written work products, leadership of two client interviews or counseling sessions and two negotiations, and evidence of professional-responsibility competence. Examiners independently assess written work using published rubrics; interpersonal-skills scoring draws on supervisor rubrics and participant reflections. Portfolio completion substitutes for examination passage, not other eligibility safeguards. The distinction concerns assessment design, not a demonstrated difference in competence outcomes.

kps.k: The frameworks extend client protections to new entrants and specify what happens when their authority becomes insufficient.
kps.d: Texas requires written disclosure of nonlawyer status and limited scope, applies confidentiality, candor, conflict and privilege protections, and requires protective steps when matters exceed permitted activities. Work wholly outside scope triggers withdrawal or addition of a lawyer in charge. Arizona places alternative business structures and their members, as well as paraprofessionals, within disciplinary jurisdiction and extends complaint procedures to them; lawyers and paraprofessionals share the stated funds-compliance duties. Oregon automatically suspends provisional authority when approved supervision or required insurance lapses and requires client notification and protection. These provisions make continuing compliance part of the delivery model.

kps.k: Implementation requires supervisory capacity, developmental opportunities and regulatory administration—not just permission to enter.
kps.d: Oregon requires supervisor training, regular feedback, workload accommodation and personal professional responsibility, with client needs taking precedence over program completion. Employers must allow time for requirements that do not directly benefit them, though compensation obligations have limits. Approved negotiation alternatives, reasonable accommodations and confidential ombudsperson support address participation barriers. Texas requires ongoing ethics and subject education and client-service reporting. Practically, participating employers and regulators must organize training, assessment, supervision and compliance processes alongside service delivery.

kps.k: The evidence establishes regulatory designs, not their effectiveness or a resolved debate about access and quality.
kps.d: The supplied provisions report no comparative costs, client outcomes, access gains or stakeholder disagreements. Their differences should not be recast as opposing empirical claims. Texas’s material concerns preliminary approval, and its court-access-assistant excerpts do not establish that role’s full scope. Oregon expressly requires annual scoring-consistency audits, whole-portfolio minimum-competence review and participant and provider feedback, with possible rubric or rule revisions. Those duties create a process for examining performance; they do not establish that the portfolio route already delivers reliable assessment or better access.

vlens.an: The selected regulators, courts and professional bodies support the proposition that alternative routes can expand legal practice without abandoning licensing, competence controls or accountability. Across the sources, authorization is conditional rather than deregulatory: Texas licenses nonlawyers only for bounded services and eligible low-income clients, Oregon substitutes a supervised practice portfolio for examination passage while retaining admission safeguards, and Arizona brings legal paraprofessionals and alternative business structures within formal licensing and disciplinary systems. Their common logic is that changed entry, scope or ownership rules should be paired with defined authority, competence assessment, professional duties, client-protection procedures and regulatory enforcement. Material variation lies in what each framework changes and how safeguards operate. Texas focuses on limited nonlawyer practice, including scope screening, selective lawyer supervision and escalation when a matter exceeds authorization. Oregon concerns an alternative route to lawyer admission, emphasizing supervised experience, portfolio assessment, insurance, feedback and continuing review of assessment consistency. Arizona addresses both nonlawyer licensure and provider governance, emphasizing institutional licensing and Supreme Court disciplinary jurisdiction. These are therefore complementary but non-interchangeable designs. The sources establish operative or preliminary regulatory frameworks, not empirical evidence that they improve access, reduce costs or maintain quality in practice; Texas is preliminary, while Oregon expressly provides for later quality review. This assessment describes only the curated sources supplied and should not be treated as representative of all regulators, courts or professional bodies.

elens.an: The Arizona rulemaking source supports the proposition that expanded legal-service models can remain subject to formal licensing and accountability rather than deregulation. It assigns alternative business structure licensure to a designated committee and places licensed legal paraprofessionals under Arizona Supreme Court disciplinary jurisdiction and delegated State Bar authority. It also distinguishes the two regulated categories administratively while integrating them into established disciplinary, complaint and financial-compliance mechanisms. Because this time-period evidence consists of one operative legal source, there is no meaningful cross-source disagreement to assess; the principal internal variation is between entity-level licensing for alternative business structures and individual licensure for legal paraprofessionals. The source does not address automation directly and provides no empirical evidence that these arrangements improve access, affordability, competence or client outcomes, so its support is confined to the feasibility and design of accountable alternatives.

elens.an: The selected 2023–2024 sources support the proposition that expanding routes into legal practice can preserve licensing, competence controls and client protection rather than amount to deregulation. Texas creates a court-licensed, subject-bounded nonlawyer route for low-income clients, with disclosure, scope limits, selective lawyer supervision, escalation duties and discipline. Oregon creates a supervised portfolio route to lawyer admission, replacing examination passage with documented practical work and assessment while retaining character-and-fitness review, insurance, supervisory responsibility and suspension safeguards. Their common logic is controlled expansion backed by defined competence and continuing accountability. Material variation lies in what boundary each changes: Texas expands who may independently deliver specified legal services, whereas Oregon changes how prospective lawyers demonstrate readiness for admission. Texas is preliminary and access-targeted; Oregon is final, practice-based and includes ongoing review of assessment consistency. Neither source reports comparative access, cost, competence or client-outcome evidence, so the period supports the proposition at the level of regulatory design, not demonstrated effectiveness. Because these are curated regulatory sources, their agreement should not be treated as evidence of prevalence or consensus, and neither attributes the reforms to generative AI despite their timing within the generative-shock period.
